mainTopic: Leaving מצרים with wealth, and the time for the morning שמע and joining גאולה to תפלה
overview: The amud opens by finishing an אגדה from the previous daf. ה׳ said 'please' when He asked Israel to take wealth from מצרים, so that אברהם would not say only half of His promise was kept. Israel would have been happy just to leave, like a prisoner who wants freedom today more than money tomorrow. The גמרא then explains how the wealth was taken, and also explains two doubled phrases: the double אהיה at the burning bush, and אליהו's double 'answer me'. A new משנה follows, giving the earliest and latest times for the morning שמע. The גמרא explains the sign of telling תכלת from white, and brings more signs from a ברייתא. אביי rules that the time for תפילין follows אחרים, but the ideal for שמע is the ותיקין way: finish at sunrise and join גאולה directly to תפלה. The גמרא praises this joining, then asks how it is possible when ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said in between, and answers with רבי אלעזר and רב אשי. Finally it explains why יהיו לרצון comes after the eighteen ברכות, which leads to proof that chapters 1 and 2 of תהלים count as one. Another proof begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: אברהם must not say only half the promise was kept
steps.stepSummary: This finishes a sentence that began on the previous daf. ה׳ asked Israel to take wealth from מצרים so that אברהם would not complain that the slavery came true but the wealth did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: [So that] that righteous man (אברהם) [should not say]: 'They will enslave them and afflict them' was fulfilled for them, but 'and afterward they will go out with great wealth' was not fulfilled for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a sentence from the previous daf. It explains why ה׳ said 'please' when He asked Israel to borrow from the Egyptians: so that אברהם would not complain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the ברית בין הבתרים, ה׳ promised אברהם two things: slavery, and after it, great wealth. The slavery had clearly come true. ה׳ wanted the wealth to come true too, so that no part of His promise to אברהם would be left unkept.

keyTerms.meaning: That righteous man, meaning אברהם אבינו
'They will enslave them and afflict them' (בראשית טו:יג)

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'should not say' (שלא יאמר) are at the end of the previous daf, so they are not printed here. Read this line as: 'so that that righteous man should not say...'

phrases.english: that righteous man (Avraham) [should not say]:
phrases.notes: This continues 'שלא יאמר' from the end of 9a.

phrases.english: 'And they will enslave them and afflict them' — He fulfilled for them,

phrases.aramaic: ״וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן יֵצְאוּ בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל״ — לֹא קִייֵּם בָּהֶם.
phrases.english: but 'and afterward they will go out with great wealth' — He did not fulfill for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This completes the explanation from דבי רבי ינאי on 9a about why ה׳ said 'דבר נא' (please speak).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ urged Israel to take the wealth so that the second half of His promise to אברהם would also be kept.

steps.title: Israel says: we just want to get out
steps.stepSummary: Israel answers משה that they would be happy just to leave, even without any wealth.
steps.simpleTranslation: They (Israel) said to him (משה): If only we could get out ourselves!
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues with Israel's reaction. This explains why ה׳ had to say 'please': the people were not eager to delay for the wealth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a new fact: Israel did not care about the wealth. All they wanted was freedom. That is why ה׳ had to ask them politely to take it.

keyTerms.meaning: Ourselves, just our own bodies (with nothing else)

phrases.english: They (Israel) said to him (Moshe):
If only we could get out ourselves!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This gives Israel's response to the request to take wealth.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Israel preferred leaving right away over leaving with wealth.

steps.title: The parable of the prisoner
steps.stepSummary: A prisoner offered freedom plus money tomorrow begs to be freed today with nothing. Israel felt the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: A parable: to a man locked in prison. People tell him: 'We will take you out of prison tomorrow and give you lots of money.' He says to them: 'Please, take me out today, and I don't want anything.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a parable (משל) to help us understand why Israel did not care about the wealth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who is suffering wants relief now, not riches later. This shows why Israel's answer was natural. It also shows why ה׳ had to say 'please' to get them to take the wealth.

phrases.aramaic: מָשָׁל: לְאָדָם שֶׁהָיָה חָבוּשׁ בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים
phrases.english: A parable: to a man who was locked in prison,
and people were saying to him:
'We will take you out of prison tomorrow,
and give you a lot of money.'
And he says to them: 'Please, I beg you,
take me out today, and I don't ask for anything.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מָשָׁל: לְאָדָם שֶׁהָיָה חָבוּשׁ בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This illustrates Israel's statement with a parable.
steps.raayaObject: Israel's preference to leave immediately, with no wealth.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A parable from ordinary human experience: a prisoner wants freedom now more than money later.
steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ said 'please' because Israel only wanted freedom. ה׳ still wanted to keep His full promise of רכוש גדול to אברהם.

steps.title: רבי אמי: the goods were given against their will
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי explains the word 'ויַּשְׁאִלוּם' to mean that the goods were lent to Israel against someone's will.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they lent them' — רבי אמי said: This teaches that they lent them against their will.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new pasuk about the wealth (שמות יב:לו). רבי אמי says the lending happened 'against their will'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pasuk says the Egyptians 'lent' to Israel. רבי אמי reads into this that the lending was not fully willing. He does not say whose will it was against, so the next step will deal with that.

phrases.english: 'And they lent them' — Rabbi Ami said:
This teaches that they lent them against their will.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This shifts from why ה׳ asked for the wealth to how the wealth was actually transferred.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The goods were lent 'against their will'.

steps.title: Whose will was it against?
steps.stepSummary: Two opinions: the goods were given against the Egyptians' will, or against Israel's will.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: against the will of the Egyptians. And some say: against the will of Israel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two ways to understand רבי אמי's unclear word 'their'. This sets up the next two steps, which give each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Against their will' could mean the Egyptians did not want to give. It could also mean Israel did not want to take. Each reading paints a very different picture of the event.
steps.confusionAlert: The second opinion, 'against Israel's will', does not mean Israel refused to take the goods. It means Israel did take them, but reluctantly, only because they were told to. On this view, it was Israel, not the Egyptians, who did not want the transfer.

phrases.english: Some say: against the will of the Egyptians,
and some say: against the will of Israel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This clarifies who 'they' are in רבי אמי's statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute whether 'against their will' refers to מצרים or ישראל.

steps.title: Source for 'against the Egyptians' will'
steps.stepSummary: The opinion that it was against מצרים's will cites the pasuk 'ונות בית תחלק שלל'. It treats the goods as spoils taken from an enemy.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says 'against the will of the Egyptians' — as it is written: 'And she who stays at home divides the spoils.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the proof for the first opinion. It is a pasuk from תהלים that calls the wealth 'spoils'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Spoils are taken from an enemy against the enemy's will. Since the pasuk calls Israel's wealth 'spoils', the Egyptians must not have wanted to give it.

phrases.english: The one who says 'against the will of the Egyptians' —
as it is written: 'And she who stays at home divides the spoils' (Psalms 68:13).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This supports the first side of the dispute.
steps.raayaObject: That the goods were given against the Egyptians' will.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים סח:יג, which calls the wealth 'שלל' (spoils).

steps.title: Reason for 'against Israel's will': the heavy load
steps.stepSummary: The opinion that it was against Israel's will explains that Israel did not want to carry heavy goods on their journey.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says 'against the will of Israel' — because of the load.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason for the second opinion. Israel did not want the extra weight to carry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This side does not use a pasuk. It uses simple logic: carrying heavy goods on a long trip is a burden. This fits the earlier steps, where Israel just wanted to leave and did not care about wealth.

keyTerms.meaning: A load, a heavy burden to carry

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אמי says the goods were lent 'against their will'. One view says it was against מצרים's will, because the pasuk calls them spoils. The other view says it was against Israel's will, because the goods were a heavy load to carry.

phrases.english: The one who says 'against the will of Israel' —
[says so] because of the load.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This supports the second side of the dispute, in parallel to step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That the goods were taken against Israel's will.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Practical reasoning: the burden of carrying heavy goods on the journey.

steps.title: רבי אמי: מצרים was left like a trap with no grain
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי explains וינצלו את מצרים to mean that Israel left מצרים like a bird trap with no grain inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And they emptied מצרים." רבי אמי said: This teaches that they made it like a trap that has no grain in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the end of the same pasuk, וינצלו את מצרים. רבי אמי explains it with a picture: מצרים became like a bird trap with no grain left as bait.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A trap works only when it holds grain to draw the birds in. רבי אמי is saying that once Israel took the wealth, מצרים had nothing left to attract anyone.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches (this word in the pasuk teaches us)

phrases.english: "And they emptied Egypt."
phrases.notes: The end of the same pasuk discussed in the previous steps (שמות יב:לו).

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said:
This teaches that they made it like a trap
that has no grain in it,
phrases.notes: Grain is the bait that draws birds into the trap.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי מְלַמֵּד שֶׁעֲשָׂאוּהָ כִּמְצוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the same pasuk (וישאלום), now focusing on its last words, וינצלו את מצרים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Israel left מצרים as empty as a trap with no grain.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: מצרים was left like deep water with no fish
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש gives a different picture: מצרים became like the deep sea with no fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: And ריש לקיש said: They made it like the depths of the sea with no fish in it.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש offers his own picture for the same words. Israel left מצרים like deep water that has no fish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both אמוראים agree that מצרים was left completely empty. They only differ in the picture they use. Fish live naturally in the sea, so this image suggests that even wealth that 'belonged' in מצרים was gone.

keyTerms.meaning: The deep part of the sea
An אמורא, the study partner of רבי יוחנן

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse the two similar-sounding words. רבי אמי says מצודה with דגן (trap, grain). ריש לקיש says מצולה with דגים (deep sea, fish).

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
They made it like the depths of the sea
that has no fish in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, parallel picture of the same idea that רבי אמי expressed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Israel left מצרים as empty as a sea with no fish.

steps.title: God's first message: I was with you and will be with you again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains אהיה אשר אהיה. הקב״ה told משה to say: I am with you in this slavery, and I will be with you in future exiles.
steps.simpleTranslation: "I will be what I will be." הקב״ה said to משה: Go tell Israel, I was with you in this slavery, and I will be with you in the slavery under the kingdoms.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new pasuk from the burning bush, אהיה אשר אהיה. It explains why the word אהיה appears twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each אהיה stands for a different time. The first means 'I am with you now in מצרים.' The second means 'I will also be with you in future exiles under other nations.' This step sets up משה's reaction in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: I will be what I will be (a name of God told to משה)
The kingdoms (the future exiles under foreign nations)

phrases.english: "I will be what I will be":

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה,
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:
Go and tell Israel:
I was with you in this slavery,
and I will be with you in the slavery of the kingdoms.
phrases.notes: This refers to the later exiles.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה לֵךְ אֱמוֹר לָהֶם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new Aggadic topic: a doubled phrase from the story of the burning bush.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The double אהיה refers to God being with Israel both now and in future exiles.

steps.title: משה objects: one hardship at a time is enough
steps.stepSummary: משה argues that it is enough to deal with the current suffering. Israel does not need to hear about future exiles now.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said before Him: Master of the World, a trouble is enough in its own time.
steps.whatsHappening: משה pushes back against the message from the previous step. He argues that people who are already suffering should not be told about suffering still to come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה does not deny that the future exiles will happen. His point is about what to say right now. Telling slaves about more slavery ahead would discourage them instead of comforting them.

keyTerms.meaning: A trouble is enough in its own time (deal with it when it comes)

phrases.english: He (Moshe) said before Him:
Master of the World,
a trouble is enough in its own time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: משה pushes back against the message described in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plan to tell Israel about future exiles
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mentioning future suffering would only add pain to people who are already suffering now.

steps.title: God agrees: just say 'אהיה sent me'
steps.stepSummary: הקב״ה accepts משה's point. He tells משה to say only 'אהיה sent me to you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: הקב״ה said to him: Go tell them, "אהיה has sent me to you."
steps.whatsHappening: הקב״ה agrees with משה. He tells him to give Israel the shorter message, with only one אהיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains a puzzle in the pasuk itself. In one part of the pasuk God says אהיה twice, but in the message משה is told to deliver, it appears only once. The second אהיה, which hinted at future exiles, was left out because of משה's request.

keyTerms.meaning: אהיה has sent me to you

steps.whatToRemember: The double אהיה means 'with you now, and with you in later exiles.' משה argued 'דיה לצרה בשעתה,' and God agreed, so Israel was told only the single אהיה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This line explains why the pasuk changes from a double אהיה to a single one. It also teaches a lasting lesson: do not burden people who are suffering with worries about the future.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him:
Go and tell them:
"I will be has sent me to you."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֵךְ אֱמוֹר לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves משה's objection by changing the message he is to deliver.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Acceptance of the objection: the message is shortened
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Israel would be told about both the current and the future exiles.
steps.terutzMaskana: Israel is told only the single אהיה, so they are not burdened with future suffering.

steps.title: Why did אליהו say 'answer me' twice?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו asks why אליהו repeated the word ענני in his prayer on הר הכרמל.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Answer me, ה׳, answer me." רבי אבהו said: Why did אליהו say 'answer me' two times?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another doubled phrase, this time from אליהו's prayer. רבי אבהו asks why the word is repeated, which sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption is that a repeated word in a pasuk must teach something extra. The question prepares us to look for two separate requests.

phrases.english: "Answer me, ה׳, answer me."
phrases.notes: מלכים א יח:לז, at הר הכרמל.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu said:
Why did Eliyahu say
'answer me' two times?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָמָה אָמַר אֵלִיָּהוּ עֲנֵנִי שְׁתֵּי פְּעָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new example of a doubled phrase, following the double אהיה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the repeated word ענני comes to teach

steps.title: Two requests: fire from heaven, and no claim of sorcery
steps.stepSummary: The first ענני asks for fire to come down. The second asks that the people not explain the fire away as כישוף.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches that אליהו said before הקב״ה: Master of the World, answer me that fire will come down from heaven and eat everything on the altar. And answer me that You will turn their minds away, so they will not say it was sorcery.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers his own question. Each ענני is a separate request.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A miracle alone was not enough. People might still deny it by calling it witchcraft. So אליהו asked for a second thing: that God would stop the people from thinking up such an excuse, so they would truly accept the miracle.

keyTerms.meaning: That You will turn their minds away (from doubting)

phrases.english: This teaches that Eliyahu said
before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the World,
"Answer me": that fire will come down from heaven
and consume everything that is on the altar;
and "answer me": that You will turn their minds away,
so that they will not say
that they are acts of sorcery.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁאָמַר אֵלִיָּהוּ לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first ענני asks for the fire. The second asks that the people not dismiss the miracle as כישוף.

steps.title: Proof from the pasuk: 'You turned their hearts backward'
steps.stepSummary: The end of אליהו's pasuk shows that turning the people's hearts was part of his request.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: "And You have turned their hearts backward."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the second request with words from the same pasuk. Those words show that אליהו was concerned with the people's hearts, not only with the fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase about turning their hearts shows that God controls what people think. That supports the idea that אליהו asked God to guide their minds away from claiming sorcery.
steps.whatToRemember: Two doubled phrases are explained here. The double אהיה means 'now and in the future,' but only one was said, because of משה's request. The double ענני means one request for the fire and one request that the people believe it.

phrases.english: As it is stated:
"And You have turned their hearts backward."

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחוֹרַנִּית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a pasuk to support the second request described in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That the second ענני was a request about the people's minds
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א יח:לז, "ואתה הסבת את לבם אחרנית"

steps.title: When the morning שמע begins
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks when the morning שמע may begin. The first opinion says it begins when one can tell תכלת from white. רבי אליעזר says it begins when one can tell תכלת from leek-green.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: From when may we say שמע in the morning? From when a person can tell the difference between sky-blue and white. רבי אליעזר says: between sky-blue and leek-green.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets the earliest time for saying the morning שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is how much daylight there is: once it is light enough to tell similar colors apart, 'when you rise' (ובקומך) has begun. רבי אליעזר picks two colors that look even more alike, blue and green. So his time is a bit later, because you need more light.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה; the label that marks the start of a new משנה

phrases.aramaic: מַתְנִי׳ מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בְּשַׁחֲרִית?
phrases.english: MISHNAH: From when do we recite Shema in the morning?
From when one can distinguish between sky-blue and white.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: בֵּין תְּכֵלֶת לְכָרָתֵי.
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: between sky-blue and leek-green.
phrases.notes: These two colors are closer to each other, so more light is needed to tell them apart.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בְּשַׁחֲרִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It is not connected to the אגדה about משה and אליהו that came before.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The morning שמע begins once there is enough light to tell תכלת from white. רבי אליעזר says it begins once one can tell תכלת from leek-green.

steps.title: When the morning שמע must be finished
steps.stepSummary: The first opinion says one must finish by sunrise. רבי יהושע says one has until three hours into the day, because kings get up at that time.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one finishes it by sunrise. רבי יהושע says: until three hours, because it is the way of kings to get up at three hours.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues and gives the latest time for the morning שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion ends the time at הנץ החמה, sunrise. רבי יהושע stretches it to three hours because 'when you rise' includes the time when important people such as kings get up. Since some people still rise then, it still counts as rising time.

keyTerms.meaning: Sunrise, when the sun starts to shine

phrases.english: And one finishes it until sunrise,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר עַד שָׁלֹשׁ שָׁעוֹת,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says: until three hours,
for such is the way of kings
to rise at three hours.
phrases.notes: Kings sleep late, so their wake-up time is the last edge of 'when you rise.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the start time, the משנה now gives the end time.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first opinion says to finish by sunrise. רבי יהושע says one has until three hours of the day.

steps.title: Reading שמע after its time
steps.stepSummary: Someone who says שמע after the deadline has not lost out. He is like someone learning Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who reads from then on has not lost. He is like a person reading in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends by telling us what happens if someone says שמע after the time is over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He has missed the מצוה of קריאת שמע at its proper time. But the words are Torah, so he still gets the reward of learning Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: From here onward, meaning after the deadline
Like one who reads the Torah

steps.whatToRemember: The morning שמע starts when there is enough light to tell similar colors apart. It ends at sunrise, or at three hours according to רבי יהושע. Saying it later still earns the reward of learning Torah.
steps.confusionAlert: 'לא הפסיד' does NOT mean he did the מצוה of קריאת שמע. It only means he still gets the reward of learning Torah.

phrases.english: One who reads from this point onward —
has not lost,
he is like a person who reads in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what happens if someone misses the end time given in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying שמע after its time misses the מצוה, but it still earns the reward of learning Torah.

steps.title: What does 'between תכלת and white' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the משנה means by telling תכלת apart from white.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is 'between sky-blue and white'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks the משנה's opening phrase to be explained. This question sets up the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה did not say which white and blue things it means. The answer matters, because a different case would mean a different amount of light and a different start time.

keyTerms.meaning: The גמרא's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is 'between sky-blue and white'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first rule of the משנה (step 16) and asks what it means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which blue and white things does the משנה have in mind?

steps.title: Not two separate piles of wool
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests it means a pile of white wool next to a pile of blue wool. It rejects this, because you could tell those apart even at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it means between a pile of white wool and a pile of blue wool, people can tell those apart even at night!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one possible meaning and shows that it cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two separate piles of different colors are easy to tell apart even in very dim light. If that were the test, it would already be met at night, so it could not mark the start of the day. The test must be something harder.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that will be rejected)

phrases.english: If you say: between a pile of white wool
and a pile of sky-blue wool —
but at night too, people can tell them apart!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to the question in step 19 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the משנה means two separate piles of wool.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That difference is visible even at night, so it cannot mark when the day begins.

steps.title: The blue and white on the same item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the משנה means the blue and white found on the same item, which are much harder to tell apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means between the blue in it and the white in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct meaning: telling apart blue and white that are close together on one item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the two colors sit right next to each other on one thing, you need real daylight to tell them apart. Sefaria understands 'it' as ציצית, with its blue and white strings. רש״י explains it as one tuft of blue-dyed wool, with spots where the dye did not fully take.

keyTerms.meaning: That is in it, on the same item

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, בֵּין תְּכֵלֶת שֶׁבָּהּ לְלָבָן שֶׁבָּהּ.
phrases.english: Rather: between the sky-blue that is in it and the white that is in it.
phrases.notes: 'In it' means ציצית (Sefaria), or a single dyed tuft with undyed spots (רש״י).

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, בֵּין תְּכֵלֶת שֶׁבָּהּ לְלָבָן שֶׁבָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading from step 20 with the correct one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה means blue and white on the same item, which needs real daylight to tell apart.

steps.title: A ברייתא gives more signs of morning
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings three more opinions. רבי מאיר says morning starts when one can tell a wolf from a dog. רבי עקיבא says when one can tell a donkey from a wild donkey. אחרים say when one can recognize a friend four אמות away.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי מאיר says, from when one can tell a wolf from a dog. רבי עקיבא says, a donkey from a wild donkey. אחרים say, from when one sees his friend four אמות away and recognizes him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא with other signs for when the morning שמע may begin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each sign is a pair of things that look alike, so telling them apart shows there is enough light. The opinions differ in how much light they require. אחרים use a person's face: being able to recognize an acquaintance from a short distance.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Meir says:
From when one can distinguish between a wolf and a dog.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: בֵּין חֲמוֹר לְעָרוֹד.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: between a donkey and a wild donkey.
And Acherim say: from when one sees his fellow
four cubits away and recognizes him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: מִשֶּׁיַּכִּיר בֵּין זְאֵב לְכֶלֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds opinions from a ברייתא about the start time from step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Other signs for the start of the morning שמע: wolf and dog (רבי מאיר), donkey and wild donkey (רבי עקיבא), or recognizing a friend four אמות away (אחרים).

steps.title: רב הונא rules like אחרים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that the הלכה follows אחרים: morning begins when you can recognize a friend four אמות away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: The law follows אחרים.
steps.whatsHappening: After hearing all the opinions about when morning begins, רב הונא gives a practical ruling. He says we follow אחרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אחרים set the start of morning at the point when you can recognize a friend four אמות away. רב הונא picks this opinion as the הלכה, but he does not say which מצוה it applies to. The next step will add that detail.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Others', an unnamed תנא whose opinion appeared in the ברייתא

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The law is like Acherim.
phrases.notes: That is, morning starts when you can recognize a friend from four amos away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules between the opinions listed in the ברייתא of step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows אחרים: morning begins when one can recognize a friend at four אמות.

steps.title: אביי splits the ruling between תפילין and שמע
steps.stepSummary: אביי says אחרים' time applies to תפילין. For קריאת שמע, the best practice is that of the ותיקין, who finished שמע exactly at sunrise, as רבי יוחנן reported.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: For תפילין, follow אחרים. For קריאת שמע, follow the ותיקין. As רבי יוחנן said: The ותיקין would finish it right at sunrise.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי sharpens רב הונא's ruling. He says it applies to putting on תפילין, while for שמע there is a better, more careful practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For תפילין, אחרים' time tells you the earliest point you may put them on. For שמע, אביי points to the ותיקין, who timed שמע so that they finished it exactly as the sun rose. רבי יוחנן's report is quoted as the source for what the ותיקין did.

keyTerms.meaning: תפילין, a מצוה done only in the daytime
Especially careful, pious people who did מצוות in the best way
Sunrise, the moment the sun appears

steps.confusionAlert: The ותיקין time is not the earliest time you are allowed to say שמע. It is the ideal, extra-careful way to do it: you finish שמע right at sunrise.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the famous practice of davening 'ותיקין' (נץ מנין), where שמונה עשרה begins right at sunrise.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
For tefillin, follow Acherim.
phrases.notes: This sets the earliest time to put on tefillin.

phrases.english: For reading Shema, follow the vasikin.
As Rabbi Yochanan said:
The vasikin would finish it (Shema)
right at sunrise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רב הונא's general ruling so that it applies to תפילין, and sets a better standard for שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפילין: follow אחרים. קריאת שמע: ideally finish right at sunrise like the ותיקין.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the ותיקין practice and explains it
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא confirms that the ותיקין finished שמע at sunrise. The reason was to join גאולה to תפלה and to daven שמונה עשרה in the daytime.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught in a ברייתא: The ותיקין would finish שמע right at sunrise, so that they would join the blessing of redemption to prayer, and so they would end up praying in the daytime.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as רבי יוחנן. The ברייתא also explains why the ותיקין did this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives two goals. First, the ברכה of גאולה, said right after שמע, should lead straight into שמונה עשרה with no break. Second, timing שמע to end exactly at sunrise makes שמונה עשרה start in full daytime, while שמע itself is still said slightly before sunrise.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was also taught this way', which introduces a ברייתא as support
The ברכה of redemption (גאל ישראל) said after שמע
Joining the גאולה ברכה directly to שמונה עשרה

phrases.english: It was also taught this way (in a Baraita):
The vasikin would finish it
right at sunrise,
so that one would join redemption to prayer,
and he ends up praying in the daytime.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יוחנן's report with a Tannaitic source and adds the reason behind it.
steps.raayaObject: The ותיקין practice of finishing שמע at sunrise
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that records the same practice and explains it

steps.title: רבי זירא finds a verse for the practice
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא brings a פסוק from תהלים as a hint for the ותיקין practice: 'They shall fear You with the sun.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: What is the verse for this? 'They shall fear You with the sun, and before the moon, for all generations.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks where this practice is hinted at in תנ"ך. He answers with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'יראוך עם שמש' are read as 'they will fear You together with the sun.' This means showing fear of Heaven, through שמע and תפלה, at the very moment the sun comes up. The question is part of רבי זירא's own statement, not a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is its verse?' This asks for the scriptural source.
'They shall fear You with the sun' (תהלים ע"ב:ה)

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
What is the verse (for this)?
'They shall fear You with the sun,'
phrases.notes: Fear of Heaven is expressed together with sunrise.

phrases.english: 'and before the moon, for all generations.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a scriptural hint to the ותיקין practice described in steps 24 and 25.
steps.raayaObject: Davening at sunrise like the ותיקין

steps.title: Joining redemption to prayer protects all day
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בן אליקים testifies, in the name of the holy community in ירושלים, that whoever joins גאולה to תפלה will not be harmed that whole day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בן אליקים testified in the name of the holy community in ירושלים: Whoever joins redemption to prayer is not harmed the entire day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a promise of reward for joining גאולה to תפלה. The next step challenges this promise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 24 and 25 gave the reason for the ותיקין practice. This step adds that the practice brings protection. The reward is for the act of joining גאולה to תפלה with no break.

keyTerms.meaning: Testified, meaning he passed on a reliable tradition
The holy community in ירושלים, a known group of חכמים

steps.whatToRemember: For תפילין, morning starts when you can recognize a friend at four אמות (אחרים). For שמע, the ideal is the ותיקין way: finish שמע at sunrise and go straight from גאולה into שמונה עשרה. Whoever joins גאולה to תפלה is protected all day.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei ben Elyakim testified
in the name of the holy community in Jerusalem:
Whoever joins redemption to prayer
is not harmed the entire day.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵעִיד רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן אֶלְיָקִים מִשּׁוּם קְהָלָא קַדִּישָׁא דְבִירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the reward for the practice whose reason was given in step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who joins גאולה to תפלה is protected from harm all day.

steps.title: רבי זירא says he joined them and was still harmed
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא challenges the promise of step 27 from his own experience: he joined גאולה to תפלה and was still harmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: Is that really true? I joined גאולה to תפלה, and I was still harmed!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא attacks the promise that joining גאולה to תפלה protects a person all day, using his own life as a counter-example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 promised: no harm all that day. רבי זירא says he did exactly that, and something bad still happened to him. So either the promise is wrong, or his 'harm' needs to be explained.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (a challenge formula doubting a statement)
I joined (I placed גאולה right next to תפלה)

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
Is that so?!
But I myself joined (redemption to prayer)
and I was harmed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the promise of protection given in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי בן אליקים's claim that one who joins גאולה to תפלה is not harmed all day.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A real-life counter-example: רבי זירא did the act and was still harmed.

steps.title: Your harm was really a privilege
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בן אליקים answers that רבי זירא's 'harm', being made to bring a myrtle gift to the king, was really an honor worth paying for.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What was your harm? That you had to bring a myrtle to the king's palace? There too, you should have been willing to pay money just to see the king's face!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא is told that what he calls 'harm' was not harm at all, so the promise still stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא was forced to join a group bringing a myrtle crown to the king, which he did not want. The answer flips it: seeing a king is so valuable that people would pay for it. So he got a free benefit, not a harm.

keyTerms.meaning: Myrtle (here, a gift brought to the king)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי זירא was harmed and the גמרא just accepts it. The answer is that this event does not count as harm at all, so the promise of step 27 is not broken.

phrases.english: He (Rabbi Yosei ben Elyakim) said to him:
How were you harmed?
That you brought a myrtle to the king's palace?
There too, you should have
paid a fee in order to see the face of the king,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's challenge by redefining his experience.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the event was a benefit, not a harm.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being forced to go to the king's palace was a harm, so the promise failed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seeing the king is a privilege worth paying for, so no harm happened and the promise stands.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: always run to see kings
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's teaching proves that seeing a king, even a non-Jewish king, is a real privilege.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוחנן said: A person should always try to run to greet the kings of Israel. And not only kings of Israel, but even kings of the nations, so that if he merits it, he will see the difference between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from רבי יוחנן for the claim that seeing a king is something valuable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן says to make an effort to see even non-Jewish kings. The reason: if a person lives to see the גאולה, he will be able to compare and see how much greater the Jewish king's glory is. This backs up the answer that רבי זירא gained, not lost.

keyTerms.meaning: Kings of the nations of the world
He will distinguish / tell the difference

phrases.english: as Rabbi Yochanan said:
A person should always strive
to run to greet the kings of Israel.
And not only to greet the kings of Israel,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: but even to greet the kings of the nations of the world,
so that if he merits (to see the redemption),

phrases.aramaic: יַבְחִין בֵּין מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם!
phrases.english: he will distinguish between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations of the world!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לְעוֹלָם יִשְׁתַּדֵּל אָדָם לָרוּץ לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the claim in step 29 that seeing a king is a privilege.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that seeing a king is a benefit, so רבי זירא was not harmed.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's teaching to run to greet kings, even non-Jewish kings.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is the source for the custom of making an effort to see a king or head of state, even a non-Jewish one.

steps.title: רבי אלעא praises his brother רב ברונא
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעא asks עולא to greet his brother רב ברונא publicly, because he is a great man who rejoices in מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעא said to עולא: When you go there (to בבל), ask about the welfare of my brother רב ברונא in front of the whole group, because he is a great man and happy with מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement praising רב ברונא, and this sets up the next line, which shows his joy in joining גאולה to תפלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Asking about someone's welfare in front of everyone is a way to give him public honor. רבי אלעא gives two reasons he deserves it: he is a great man, and he rejoices in מצוות. The next line proves the second reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Ask about the welfare of / greet
In the presence of the whole group

phrases.english: Rabbi Ila said to Ulla:
When you go in there (to Babylonia),
ask after the welfare of my brother, Rav Beruna,
in the presence of the entire group,
for he is a great man
and he rejoices in מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אִלָּעָא לְעוּלָּא: כִּי עָיְילַתְּ לְהָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the רבי זירא exchange to a story about another sage connected to joining גאולה to תפלה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב ברונא deserves public honor because he is great and rejoices in מצוות.

steps.title: רב ברונא joined them and laughed all day
steps.stepSummary: Proof of רב ברונא's joy: once he joined גאולה to תפלה and was full of joy the entire day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once he joined גאולה to תפלה, and laughter did not stop from his mouth the whole day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב ברונא really rejoiced in מצוות, through a story about joining גאולה to תפלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He managed to join them at sunrise like the ותיקין, which is hard to time exactly. His all-day joy shows both how much he loved the מצוה and how special this practice is.

phrases.english: Once,
he joined redemption to prayer,
and laughter did not stop from his mouth
the entire day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the claim in step 31 that רב ברונא rejoices in מצוות.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of his all-day joy after joining גאולה to תפלה.

steps.title: How can you join them if you say a פסוק in between?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how joining is possible, since רבי יוחנן said we begin שמונה עשרה with ה׳ שפתי תפתח, which seems to be a break between גאולה and תפלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can a person join them? Didn't רבי יוחנן say: At the beginning one says 'ה׳ שפתי תפתח', and at the end one says 'יהיו לרצון אמרי פי'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the whole idea of joining גאולה to תפלה: we say an extra פסוק right before שמונה עשרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Joining means nothing should come between the ברכה of גאל ישראל and שמונה עשרה. But רבי יוחנן says to open with the פסוק ה׳ שפתי תפתח. That פסוק seems to be a break, so how does anyone really join them?

keyTerms.meaning: How is it possible / how can
'Lord, open my lips': the פסוק said before שמונה עשרה
'May the words of my mouth be acceptable': the פסוק said after שמונה עשרה

phrases.english: How is he able to join (them)?
But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
At the beginning (of prayer) one says:
"Lord, open my lips,"
and at the end one says:
"May the words of my mouth be acceptable, etc."!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי מָצֵי סָמֵיךְ? וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After praising the practice, the גמרא questions whether it is even possible in practice.
steps.kashyaTarget: The practice of joining גאולה to תפלה (steps 25, 27, 32).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן requires saying ה׳ שפתי תפתח before שמונה עשרה, which seems to create a break between גאולה and תפלה.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: that פסוק is only for ערבית
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר answers that ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said only at ערבית, so in the morning there is no break.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: Let it be in the ערבית prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question by limiting רבי יוחנן's rule about ה׳ שפתי תפתח to the evening prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The joining that matters most is in the morning, at שחרית. If ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said only at ערבית, then in the morning nothing comes between גאולה and תפלה, and the challenge is gone.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אלעזר is not saying we never say ה׳ שפתי תפתח in the morning in practice. He is giving one way to answer the question. The גמרא challenges this answer in step 35, and רבי אלעזר revises it in step 36.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
Let it be (said only) in the evening prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: תְּהֵא בִּתְפִלָּה שֶׁל עַרְבִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 33 by limiting where the פסוק is said.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of רבי יוחנן's rule to ערבית.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said before every שמונה עשרה, so it would break the joining at שחרית.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי אלעזר, it is said only at ערבית, so at שחרית nothing interrupts between גאולה and תפלה.

steps.title: Joining at ערבית is also praised, so the verse cannot go there
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 34. רבי יוחנן said that one who joins גאולה to תפלה at ערבית earns עולם הבא, so ערבית needs joining too.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבי יוחנן say: Who is destined for עולם הבא? The one who joins the גאולה of ערבית to the תפלה of ערבית!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave. Putting ה׳ שפתי תפתח at ערבית does not solve anything, because joining matters at ערבית too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 34 moved the verse to ערבית to avoid a break in the morning. But רבי יוחנן praises joining גאולה to תפלה specifically at ערבית. If the verse is said at night, it now causes a break exactly where joining is so highly praised.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [he] say? This introduces a contradiction.
One destined for the World to Come

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
Who is one destined for the World to Come?
This is one who joins the redemption blessing of the evening
to the prayer of the evening!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 34
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's claim that ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said only at ערבית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Joining גאולה to תפלה is praised at ערבית too, so saying the verse there would create a forbidden break.

steps.title: The verse is said at מנחה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר revises his answer. ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said at מנחה, where no גאולה comes before the תפלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי אלעזר said: Let it be said at the מנחה prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives a new answer. The verse belongs to מנחה, where nothing needs to be joined.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שחרית and ערבית both have a גאולה blessing right before שמונה עשרה, so a break there is a problem. מנחה has no גאולה blessing before it. Saying ה׳ שפתי תפתח at מנחה therefore breaks nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. This signals a replacement answer.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Elazar said:
Let it be [said] in the afternoon prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 35 by changing which prayer the verse belongs to
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting רבי יוחנן's rule to a prayer with no גאולה before it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse was said at ערבית and would break the joining there.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse is said only at מנחה, where there is no joining to break.

steps.title: A fixed addition counts as part of the prayer
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that even if ה׳ שפתי תפתח is said at all the prayers, it is not a break. The רבנן made it part of the תפלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: You can even say it is said at all of them. Since the רבנן fixed it into the תפלה, it is like an extended תפלה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a completely different answer. The verse can be said at every prayer, because it is not a break at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר avoided the problem by moving the verse to מנחה. רב אשי instead changes how we view the verse. A text the רבנן fixed as the opening of שמונה עשרה counts as the start of שמונה עשרה itself. So גאולה is still joined directly to תפלה.

keyTerms.meaning: On all of them, meaning every prayer
The Rabbis fixed it in place
It is like, it is considered

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי does not say a break is allowed. He says this verse is not a break in the first place, because it already counts as part of שמונה עשרה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why we say ה׳ שפתי תפתח before every שמונה עשרה, including שחרית, without worrying about breaking סמיכת גאולה לתפלה.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Even if you say [it is said] at all of them,
since the Rabbis fixed it into the prayer,
it is considered like an extended prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא אַכּוּלְּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the same question that רבי אלעזר answered in step 36
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the verse as part of the תפלה rather than an interruption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ה׳ שפתי תפתח is a separate text that comes between גאולה and תפלה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the רבנן fixed it into the תפלה, it counts as the תפלה itself, so there is no break at any prayer.

steps.title: Proof from השכיבנו at night
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי proves his idea. At ערבית we say השכיבנו after גאולה, and it still does not break the joining, because it counts as an extended גאולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you don't say this, how can anyone join at ערבית? He has to say השכיבנו! Rather, since the רבנן instituted השכיבנו, it is like an extended גאולה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings a proof. Everyone agrees joining is possible at ערבית, even though השכיבנו comes in the middle, so his rule must be true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At night, the blessing השכיבנו sits between the גאולה blessing and שמונה עשרה. If every added text were a break, joining at ערבית would be impossible, yet רבי יוחנן praises it. The only explanation is that a rabbinic addition becomes part of the blessing next to it.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you don't say so
The night blessing 'Help us lie down' that follows גאולה

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
at the evening prayer, how could one join?
But he must say 'Hashkiveinu'!
Rather, since the Rabbis instituted Hashkiveinu,
it is considered like an extended redemption blessing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב אשי's principle from step 37
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's rule that a rabbinic addition is considered part of the adjoining prayer or blessing
steps.raayaSupportSource: השכיבנו at ערבית, which does not break the joining of גאולה to תפלה that רבי יוחנן praises

steps.title: Applying the השכיבנו model to ה׳ שפתי תפתח
steps.stepSummary: Just as השכיבנו counts as part of גאולה, ה׳ שפתי תפתח counts as part of תפלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too here: since the רבנן fixed it into the תפלה, it is like an extended תפלה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the proof back to the original question. The verse is part of the תפלה, so there is no break.
steps.deeperAnalysis: השכיבנו stretches the גאולה forward, since it comes after it. ה׳ שפתי תפתח stretches the תפלה backward, since it comes before it. Either way, גאולה flows directly into תפלה with nothing foreign in between. The גמרא repeats רב אשי's line here to close the argument.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers for ה׳ שפתי תפתח. רבי אלעזר says it belongs only to מנחה. רב אשי says it is said at every prayer and is no break, because fixed rabbinic additions count as part of the prayer. The proof is השכיבנו, which counts as an extended גאולה.

phrases.english: So too here,
since the Rabbis fixed it into the prayer,
it is considered like an extended prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי כֵּיוָן דְּקַבְעוּהָ רַבָּנַן בִּתְפִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the השכיבנו proof back to ה׳ שפתי תפתח
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ה׳ שפתי תפתח, fixed by the רבנן, is part of שמונה עשרה, so it does not break the joining of גאולה to תפלה.

steps.title: Why is the verse 'May the words of my mouth' said at the end?
steps.stepSummary: The verse יהיו לרצון אמרי פי could refer to words already said or words about to be said. So why did the רבנן place it after the שמונה עשרה ברכות instead of at the start?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, this verse, 'May the words of my mouth be acceptable,' can mean the end, about what was already said. It can also mean the beginning, about what I am about to say. So why did the רבנן set it after the eighteen ברכות? Let them say it at the beginning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the line said before the תפלה to the line said after it. It asks why יהיו לרצון was placed at the end, when it could just as well be said at the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording 'may my words be acceptable' does not make clear whether it means words already spoken or words about to be spoken. Because either reading works, the placement at the end needs a reason. The גמרא is asking for the source of the רבנן's choice.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, since (opens a line of reasoning that leads to a question)
May the words of my mouth be acceptable (תהלים יט:טו)

phrases.english: Now, since this verse 'May the words of my mouth be acceptable'
phrases.notes: The verse said at the end of the עמידה.

phrases.english: can mean the end (about words already said),
and can mean the beginning, about what I want to say.
What is the reason the רבנן established it
after the eighteen blessings?
Let them say it at the beginning!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After dealing with ה׳ שפתי תפתח at the start of the תפלה, the גמרא turns to the verse said at the end.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the רבנן placed יהיו לרצון after the eighteen ברכות rather than before them.

steps.title: דוד wrote it after eighteen chapters
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי שמעון בן פזי explains that דוד wrote this verse after eighteen chapters of תהלים. So the רבנן placed it after the eighteen ברכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה, son of רבי שמעון בן פזי, said: Since דוד only said it after eighteen chapters, the רבנן set it after the eighteen ברכות.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא answers the question. The placement of the verse in תהלים is the model for its placement in the תפלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה counts the verse as closing the eighteenth chapter of תהלים, so it is said only once eighteen chapters are complete. The רבנן matched this by putting it after the eighteen ברכות of the עמידה. Where the verse sits in תהלים decides where it sits in the prayer.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for our practice of saying יהיו לרצון at the end of the עמידה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, said:
Since David did not say it
except after eighteen chapters,
therefore the Rabbis established it
after the eighteen blessings.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹאִיל וְלֹא אֲמָרוֹ דָּוִד אֶלָּא לְאַחַר שְׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 40.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse comes after eighteen chapters of תהלים, so it is said after the eighteen ברכות.

steps.title: There are really nineteen chapters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the verse comes at the end of chapter nineteen, so nineteen chapters come before it, not eighteen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are these eighteen? They are nineteen!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the count in step 41. The verse closes chapter nineteen of תהלים, so the number does not seem to match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 41 depends on the number eighteen lining up with the eighteen ברכות. If there are really nineteen chapters, the parallel falls apart. The challenge targets the counting, not the idea of following דוד's order.

phrases.english: Are these eighteen?!
They are nineteen!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the count used in the answer of step 41.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that יהיו לרצון comes after eighteen chapters.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse ends chapter nineteen, so nineteen chapters come before it, and the match to eighteen ברכות fails.

steps.title: The first two chapters count as one
steps.stepSummary: אשרי האיש (chapter 1) and למה רגשו גוים (chapter 2) are really one chapter, so the count is eighteen after all.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Happy is the man' and 'Why are the nations in an uproar' are one chapter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It joins the first two chapters of תהלים into one, which brings the count back to eighteen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once chapters 1 and 2 count as a single chapter, the verse at the end of our chapter 19 really comes after eighteen chapters. This saves the parallel to the eighteen ברכות. The answer of step 41 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Happy is the man (opening of תהלים chapter 1)
Why are the nations in an uproar (opening of תהלים chapter 2)

steps.confusionAlert: Our printed תהלים splits these into two chapters. The גמרא is saying that in its counting they form one unit, so 'nineteen' in our numbering equals 'eighteen' in the גמרא's count.
steps.whatToRemember: יהיו לרצון is said after the עמידה because דוד placed it after eighteen chapters of תהלים, since chapters 1 and 2 count as one. This matches the eighteen ברכות.

phrases.english: 'Happy is the man' and 'Why are the nations in an uproar'
are one chapter.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ״ וְ״לָמָּה רָגְשׁוּ גוֹיִם״ חֲדָא פָּרָשָׁה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the counting challenge of step 42.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the count: two chapters are really one unit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each of the first two chapters counts separately, making nineteen.
steps.terutzMaskana: Chapters 1 and 2 are one chapter, so the verse comes after eighteen, matching the eighteen ברכות.

steps.title: דוד said 103 chapters before saying הללויה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי שמעון בן פזי teaches that דוד composed 103 chapters and did not say הללויה until he saw the downfall of the wicked, as the verse at the end of chapter 104 shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יהודה, son of רבי שמעון בן פזי, said: דוד said 103 chapters, and he did not say 'הללויה' until he saw the downfall of the wicked. As it says: 'Let sinners cease from the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless God, my soul, הללויה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching to prove its earlier claim that chapters 1 and 2 of תהלים are really one chapter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first הללויה in תהלים comes at the end of chapter 104 in our count. רבי יהודה says it came at the close of the 103rd chapter. That number fits only if two of our chapters are really one.

keyTerms.meaning: Chapters or sections, here meaning chapters of תהלים
'Praise God', a word of joyful praise
'Let sinners cease', the verse in chapter 104

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is the evidence. It also contains a lesson of its own: דוד waited to say a full הללויה until he saw the wicked fall.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, said:
phrases.notes: The same אמורא quoted in step 41, so he is consistent with himself.

phrases.english: David said one hundred and three chapters,
and he did not say 'Halleluyah'
until he saw the downfall of the wicked,
as it is stated: 'Let sinners cease from the earth,'
'and let the wicked be no more;'
'Bless the Lord, my soul, Halleluyah.'
phrases.notes: תהלים 104:35, the first הללויה in the book.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings evidence for step 43's claim that chapters 1 and 2 are one chapter.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that אשרי האיש and למה רגשו גוים are one chapter
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching that 103 chapters came before the first הללויה, which appears at the end of chapter 104

steps.title: But there are 104 chapters, not 103
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the count seems wrong. In our numbering, 104 chapters come up to that verse, not 103.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are these 103? They are 104!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the number in רבי יהודה's teaching. Counted the usual way, the verse with הללויה ends chapter 104.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of counting problem as in step 42. The גמרא raises it on purpose, because solving it will prove the earlier claim.

phrases.english: Are these one hundred and three?
They are one hundred and four!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מֵאָה וְשָׁלֹשׁ? מֵאָה וְאַרְבַּע הָוְיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the number given in step 44.
steps.kashyaTarget: The count of 103 chapters in רבי יהודה's teaching
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the standard numbering, 104 chapters come before and include the first הללויה, so 103 looks wrong.

steps.title: So chapters 1 and 2 must be one chapter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that אשרי האיש and למה רגשו גוים are one chapter, which makes the count 103. It then opens another proof from רבי שמואל בר נחמני in the name of רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn from this that 'אשרי האיש' and 'למה רגשו גוים' are one chapter. As רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יוחנן:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the counting problem: if chapters 1 and 2 are one, there are exactly 103. The last line sets up a second proof, whose content comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'שמע מינה' tell us this answer is the only way to make the number work, so it becomes proof. The same fact also solves the counting problem of step 42 (nineteen instead of eighteen). The quote from רבי יוחנן is only introduced here, and its content follows next.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Learn from this', a conclusion drawn from what was just said
'Happy is the man', the opening of תהלים chapter 1
'Why are the nations in uproar', the opening of תהלים chapter 2

steps.whatToRemember: Two separate counts (18 before יהיו לרצון, and 103 before the first הללויה) only work if chapters 1 and 2 of תהלים are one chapter.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is changing the text of תהלים. It is saying that what we split into two chapters was really counted as one section.

phrases.english: Rather, conclude from this
that 'Happy is the man' and 'Why are the nations in uproar'
are a single chapter.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
phrases.notes: This only introduces an additional proof. The content of the teaching continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves step 45's counting problem, which confirms step 43. It then introduces a further proof.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אשרי האיש and למה רגשו גוים form one chapter. This is confirmed by the 103-chapter count, with another proof to follow from רבי יוחנן.
